nameStory: Needle Spikerush gets its name from its incredibly thin, needle-like stems that look more like green acupuncture needles poking up from the water than typical plant stems. The scientific name 'acicularis' literally means 'needle-shaped' in Latin, confirming that botanists were just as struck by this plant's ultra-skinny appearance as we are today.
description: Needle Spikerush is a tiny wetland plant that looks like someone scattered green needles in shallow water or muddy ground. These grass-like stems rarely grow taller than 6 inches, sprouting from underground creeping stems called rhizomes that spread beneath the surface. Each needle-thin stem is topped with a single, sharply pointed flower spike that's smaller than your pinky nail, making this one of the most delicate members of the sedge family.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Impossibly thin, wire-like green stems that feel smooth and firm between your fingers, resembling tiny knitting needles more than plant stems

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Single tiny spike at the tip of each stem, sharply pointed and lance-shaped, less than a quarter-inch long with overlapping brownish scales

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense mats or scattered colonies of needle-like stems, rarely taller than 6 inches, often much shorter in harsh bog conditions

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: No visible leaves - what you see are the photosynthetic stems themselves, with only tiny scale-like structures at the base

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Spreads by thin underground rhizomes that feel like buried threads when you gently probe the mud with your finger

habitat: Look for Needle Spikerush in shallow water at pond edges, muddy shores of vernal pools, and boggy areas where the ground stays consistently moist. It thrives in spots where the water is only an inch or two deep, often growing alongside other tiny wetland plants in areas that dry out seasonally but never completely.

seasonality.spring: Young needle-like stems begin emerging from the mud as water levels rise, appearing as tiny green threads poking through the surface.
seasonality.summer: Stems reach full height and produce their minute flower spikes at the tips, though you'll need to look closely to notice the tiny blooms.
seasonality.fall: Stems may begin to yellow and die back, though in mild conditions some persist through early winter.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground growth disappears, but the underground rhizomes remain alive, ready to sprout new needle-stems in spring.

funFact: Needle Spikerush is so popular in the aquarium trade that it's cultivated commercially and shipped worldwide to create underwater 'grass lawns' in fish tanks - making it possibly the only New England bog plant that's more famous in pet stores than in nature guides!
confusionNotes: Among its many spikerush relatives, Needle Spikerush stands out for being by far the skinniest - if the stems look thick enough to be called 'grass-like' rather than 'needle-like,' you're probably looking at a different spikerush species. Remember: if it looks like you could thread it through a needle's eye, it's probably Needle Spikerush!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'spikerush,' this plant isn't a true rush at all but belongs to the sedge family. The 'spike' refers to the flower cluster shape, not any sharp or dangerous feature - these delicate plants couldn't hurt anything bigger than a water flea!
compareHints: Needle Spikerush is the most delicate of all New England spikerushes, with stems so thin they make other species look chunky by comparison. While Common Spikerush and Blunt Spikerush have stems thick enough to feel substantial in your fingers, Needle Spikerush stems are barely thicker than heavy thread. Its relatives also tend to grow taller and have more robust flower spikes, making Needle Spikerush the 'baby' of the spikerush family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many spikerush species in New England, blunt spikerush stands out for its soft, spongy stems and distinctly rounded spikelets.
Unlike other spikerushes that grow in shallow water or wet soil, Robbins' Spikerush is the deep-water specialist of the genus, growing fully submerged in 1-4 feet of water.

Among the many spikerush species in New England, Black-fruited Spikerush is most easily distinguished by its dark seeds - Common Spikerush has pale tan seeds, while Needle Spikerush is much more delicate with thread-like stems.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Yellow Spikerush stands out for its pale, yellowish coloring and smaller stature compared to Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.
Among New England spikerushes, common spikerush is distinguished by its robust, colony-forming habit and relatively large flower spikes.
Among New England's many spikerush species, Small Spikerush is distinguished by its extremely short stature (under 4 inches) and preference for salty habitats.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Matted Spikerush is unique for its low, mat-forming growth habit - all its relatives grow upright.
Among its many spikerush relatives in New England, ovate spikerush stands out with its distinctly oval or egg-shaped flower spikes - most other spikerushes have more cylindrical or pointed spikes.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Slender Spikerush stands out for its particularly thin stems and small, oval flower spikes.
Among New England's spikerushes, Wright's is distinguished by its small size and the distinctive pyramid-shaped tubercle on its seeds.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Horsetail Spikerush is unique for its hollow, jointed stems - most other spikerushes have solid stems without visible segments.
Among the many spikerush species in New England, squarestem spikerush is the only one with distinctly four-angled stems - all the others have round or slightly flattened stems.

Few-flower Spikerush stands out from its many spikerush relatives primarily by its sparse flower count - most other New England spikerushes like Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush have dense, crowded spikelets with dozens of flowers.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Long-tubercled Spikerush stands out for its exceptionally large tubercle - up to 2.
Beaked spikerush differs from its many spikerush relatives primarily in its habitat preferences and the distinctive beaked tubercle on its seeds.
Among New England's spikerushes, Slender Spikerush has the thinnest stems - much thinner than Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.

Among the spikerushes, Bald Spikerush stands out for its particularly wide, oval flower spikes with a reddish tint, unlike the narrow spikes of Needle Spikerush or the larger, brown spikes of Common Spikerush.

Unlike Common Spikerush which has smooth, round stems, or Needle Spikerush which forms dense mats of hair-thin stems, Threerib Spikerush is the only species in the genus with distinctly three-ribbed stems.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Creeping Spikerush is unique for its mat-forming, spreading growth pattern via underground runners.
